html:
In 105 CE the court official Cai Lun presented the Han emperor with a better way of making paper. This is the traditional date for the invention of paper, though paper itself is somewhat older.

Cai Lun's paper was made from tree bark, hemp ends, old rags and worn fishing nets, soaked and beaten into a pulp, spread on a screen and dried into sheets. The cheap, plentiful materials were the key. Before this, Chinese wrote on bamboo and wooden strips, which were heavy, or on silk, which was costly. Archaeologists have found older paper from the 2nd century BCE, but it was coarse and mostly used for wrapping.

Paper slowly replaced bamboo in China over the next centuries. It reached Korea and Japan by the 600s, and the Islamic world after the Arabs learned the craft at Samarkand in the 700s. From there it reached Europe. Without cheap paper, woodblock printing, and later the printing press, would have been of little use.
